newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Competition seen fierce in Australian power market.
newsitem.headline: Competition seen fierce in Australian power market.

text.p: Australia's fast-changing A$12 billion a year electricity industry has been presented with a picture of fierce competition in an unstable market since the recent establishment of the first phase of a national market.

As free-trade markets in electricity develop in the two main east-coast states of Victoria and New South Wales (NSW), an industry conference has also been told that in current markets it was nearly impossible to predict mid to long-term prices.

The views were presented to a two-day Gas and Electricity Risk Management conference in Sydney as Victoria and NSW completed just four weeks of electricity free-trade, without the physical limitation "throttle" on trade between the markets.

However, the conference was also told that Sydney Futures Exchange electricity futures trading, to begin in September, will improve the quality of data available to the market as it grapples with foreward pricing.

The transition to a contestable (free-bid) market was well advanced in NSW and Victoria, with customers above 750 megawatt hours (MWh) a year, including supermarkets and medium-sized factories, taking market prices from July 1, said David Cornelius, manager energy trading for Powercor Australia Ltd.

Powercor, fully owned by U.S. utility PacifiCorp, is a leading player in the two states, retailing more than 40 percent of the contestable electricity market in Victoria and holding a 60 percent stake of distribution in the western and central regions of ther state. It also holds the largest market share by an independent retailer in NSW.
"The market has been fiercely competitive," Cornelius said.
Retailers have been competing for customers largely on price, margins had been thin and risk was being underpriced to retail customers, Cornelius said.
Competition has been fierce because market share had been valued early as a measurement of success, he said.

There were also too many retailers and product differential was low, he said. However, indications that the retail market was becoming more rational were offered by a better behaved de-regulated Victorian market, now two years old, than NSW, now nine months into de-regulation, he added.
"Price, price, price -- (it is) now possible to win some customers on non-price issues but price must be close," Cornelius said in a paper presented to the conference.
Many electricity intensive customers would continue to see power as a commodity and seek only the lowest price, he said.

But it would not be sufficient to be solely an electricity retailer to small businesses and residential customers, he said. Loyalty programmes, aggregation by municipalities or brokers and use of multiple utilities could be expected, Cornelius said.

Executives of leading NSW generator Pacific Power told the conference that volatility in electricity prices could be excpected to remain, and that the cash impact of this was likely to increase as spot prices varied.
Lack of recognition of volatility could be potentially very expensive, Pacific Power's manager of energy trading, Russell Petch, and manager of marketing, Robert Murphy, said in a paper.
The paper discussed the impact of volatility on the use of electricity risk management instruments.
The present market of prices close to marginal costs was unstable, with spot prices expected to rise after mergers, takeovers or behaviour changes in the industry, they said.
It was difficult to predict whether this would happen "tomorrow or in three years time," they said.
One of their main conclusions was that technical analysis was "next to useless" in predicting mid to long-term prices.
"The current market is not in equilibrium," the paper said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
